source.title: On Generalization Error Bounds of Noisy Gradient Methods for Non-Convex Learning
source.authors: Jian Li; Xuan-Yuan Luo; Ming-Da Qiao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper runs noisy gradient methods on normal and randomly labeled image data and reports training accuracy and generalization error, bearing on fitting and label-noise behavior. Its experiments use GLD/SGLD rather than the original SGD setup.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017a) for prior observations; those cited results are not extracted as this study's results. Its own experiments compare normal and randomly labeled data. The reported generalization error is the gap between training and test 0/1 loss, not test error itself. Figure values have no numeric labels recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training-accuracy and generalization-gap experiments across label-corruption fractions using GLD/SGLD, bearing on V4. No experiment uses completely randomized labels, so these experiments do not test V1's all-random-label condition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors emphasize that their data-dependent bounds distinguish corrupted-label from normal data and track the shapes of generalization-gap curves. They do not establish the complete V1 or V4 claims.
record.recipe_differences: The original claims concern standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods; this paper studies GLD and SGLD with injected Gaussian noise. Its experiments use MLP and small AlexNet models on MNIST/CIFAR10, with sampled subsets and selected corruption portions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset/model, random-label portion, and whether gradient clipping is used; the SGLD settings and clipping condition vary across figures.

fits_no_version.finding: The accumulated squared gradient norms and the resulting theoretical bounds are larger for corrupted-label data; bound curves resemble generalization-gap curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization-path gradient norms distinguish corrupted-label training from clean-label training in these noisy-gradient experiments.

record.problems: The key experiment values are figure-only and lack recoverable numeric values in the supplied text. The paper reports a generalization gap rather than test error at chance. For the SGLD figures, it notes that the chosen learning rate exceeds the theorem's stated condition, then provides a separate gradient-clipped experiment on a 250-point subset. The authors note that the bound is greater than 1 in the reported SGLD figures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, Gaussian-noise inputs, explicit regularizers, or learning order; these versions were not tested. No omitted rows from the paper's directly relevant random-label experiments.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error in that condition, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to true-label training. The largest tested replacement fraction is 0.75.

A small constant-factor training-time comparison and convergence slowing with increasing corruption are not established. Statements about slow fitting concern injected Gaussian noise, without the required true-versus-random timing comparison.

The fully corrupted endpoint, perfect training fit across corruption fractions, steady test-error increase toward chance, and separate measurement of learning remaining signal versus memorizing noise are not established by the supplied text.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after their removal. The regularized Langevin bounds do not test these assertions.
The temporal order of fitting shared patterns and noisy labels is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text preserves axes and legends but not readable curve trajectories. Consequently, individual row states remain cannot_determine, while the narrow qualitative verdicts rely on explicit prose comparisons. Missing numerical information and untested endpoints do not justify limits_scope. The hypothetical perfect-fit example in footnote 4 is not an experimental result.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses noisy GLD/SGLD rather than standard SGD, and does not report test error at chance; it reports the train-test loss gap.

The experiments use only selected corruption portions, not a full sweep from none to all; perfect training fit at every portion and steady test-error rise are not established. The reported generalization measure is a train-test gap.

relationships.condition: Qualitative generalization-gap worsening across the tested GLD/MNIST corruption fractions
relationships.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly reports larger gaps with greater corruption (R5–R8); this supports the degradation component only, without establishing perfect fit or a test-error trajectory.
relationships.display_finding: Generalization gaps grew as label corruption increased in the GLD experiments on MNIST.

relationships.condition: Qualitative corrupted-versus-clean generalization-gap comparison in the Figure 3 SGLD settings
relationships.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly includes Figure 3 in its higher-corruption, higher-gap result (R11–R12, R15–R16, R19–R20); exact gaps and training-fit endpoints remain unreadable.
relationships.display_finding: Corrupted labels produced larger generalization gaps than clean labels in the tested SGLD settings.

relationships.condition: Qualitative corrupted-versus-clean comparison with gradient clipping on 250 MNIST examples
relationships.reason: Appendix C.2 says the random-versus-normal result persists when the bound's conditions hold (R23–R24); this supports gap worsening only.
relationships.display_finding: Random labels produced a larger generalization gap than normal labels even with gradient clipping on 250 MNIST examples.
